title: Enzymes, ATP and metabolism
blurb: Sort reactions into anabolism and catabolism, explain how ATP carries energy, and predict how temperature, pH, substrate and inhibitors change an enzyme's rate.
question: A patient who cannot digest milk sugar takes lactase tablets with meals. How does lactase speed the breakdown of lactose, why does one tablet digest a lot of lactose, and why would boiling the tablets ruin them?

teach.h: Metabolism: building up and breaking down
teach.body: Formal definition: metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism. Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones and requires energy; catabolism breaks larger molecules into smaller ones and releases energy. Metabolic pathways are chains of enzyme-controlled steps. Plain English: a cell is always both building (proteins, glycogen) and demolishing (glucose, food). The demolition pays for the building, and ATP carries the payment.

teach.caption: Hook: anabolic steroids BUILD muscle; catabolism CUTS molecules down.

teach.body: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups. Hydrolyzing the bond to the last phosphate (ATP to ADP + Pi) releases usable energy, which drives energy-requiring (endergonic) reactions: energy coupling. Catabolism, mainly cellular respiration, recharges ADP + Pi back into ATP. Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted, and every conversion loses some energy as heat.

Enzymes are biological catalysts, most of them proteins. They speed reactions by LOWERING the activation energy. They are not used up or changed, and they do not change the total energy released or the equilibrium. Each enzyme's active site binds a specific substrate (lock-and-key; in the induced-fit model the site molds slightly around it). Names usually end in -ase and name the substrate: lactase digests lactose, lipase lipids, protease proteins, amylase starch.

teach.caption: Activity rises to an optimum, then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures (its active site unfolds). Heat-denatured enzymes usually do not recover on cooling.

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Rises to the optimum, then denatures
Each enzyme has its own optimum pH
More enzyme, faster rate (if substrate is plentiful)
Metal ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺); organic helpers such as NAD+
A pathway's end product slows an early enzyme
teach.caption: pH optimums: pepsin about 2 (stomach), salivary amylase about 7 (mouth), trypsin about 8 (small intestine).

teach.body: Sofia, a patient at a clinic where nursing applicant Ray volunteers, is lactose intolerant. Digesting lactose is catabolism: lactase hydrolyzes it into glucose and galactose. The enzyme speeds this by lowering the activation energy. Because an enzyme is released unchanged after each reaction, one tablet's lactase can break down many lactose molecules. Boiling the tablets would denature the lactase: its active site would unfold, lactose would no longer fit, and cooling would not restore it.

teach.text: Exam traps: enzymes LOWER activation energy, are NOT used up and do NOT shift the equilibrium; hotter is faster only up to the optimum; each enzyme has its OWN pH optimum (pepsin is acidic); anabolism USES energy and catabolism RELEASES it; ATP has THREE phosphates and ADP two; a competitive inhibitor binds the ACTIVE site and more substrate beats it.

items: Metabolism = all reactions. Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases energy.
ATP (3 phosphates) to ADP + Pi releases energy; respiration recharges ADP into ATP.
Every energy conversion loses some energy as heat.
Enzymes lower activation energy, are reused and are specific to their substrate.
Rate depends on temperature, pH, substrate and enzyme levels; high heat denatures.
Competitive inhibitor: active site, beaten by more substrate. Noncompetitive: other site, shape change.

summary: You can now classify reactions as anabolic or catabolic, explain how ATP stores and releases energy, and describe how an enzyme's active site lowers activation energy. You can also predict how temperature, pH, substrate concentration, cofactors and competitive or noncompetitive inhibitors change enzyme activity.

A.q: How do enzymes speed up chemical reactions in the body?
options: By lowering the activation energy
By raising the reaction temperature
By adding energy to the products
By being used up as reactants
A.why: Enzymes are catalysts: they lower the activation energy needed to start a reaction.

whyNot.1: Enzymes do not heat the cell; they make the reaction easier at body temperature.
whyNot.2: Enzymes do not change the energy of the products or the total energy released.
whyNot.3: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.

A.q: How many phosphate groups does a molecule of ADP have?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
A.why: ADP is adenosine DIphosphate: two phosphates. ATP has three.

whyNot.2: Three phosphates is ATP; losing one gives ADP.
whyNot.3: Neither ATP nor ADP has four phosphate groups.

options: Building proteins from amino acids
Linking glucose units into glycogen
Breaking down glucose in respiration
Making glucose in photosynthesis
A.why: Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones and releases energy, as cellular respiration does with glucose.

whyNot.0: Protein synthesis builds a polymer and uses energy: anabolic.
whyNot.1: Glycogen formation builds a polymer from glucose: anabolic.
whyNot.3: Photosynthesis builds glucose from CO2 and water using light energy: anabolic.

B.q: Salivary amylase works best near pH 7. What happens to its activity when it reaches the stomach, at about pH 2?
options: It rises, since acid speeds up enzymes.
It falls, since the low pH alters its shape.
It stays the same, since pH has little effect.
It rises, since amylase prefers acid like pepsin.
B.why: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Far from amylase's optimum, its active site changes shape and activity falls.

whyNot.0: Acid does not speed up enzymes in general; each has its own optimum.
whyNot.2: pH strongly affects enzyme shape and activity.
whyNot.3: Pepsin has an acidic optimum, but amylase's optimum is near neutral.

B.q: Which statement describes the induced-fit model of enzyme action?
options: The substrate bends to fit a rigid active site.
Any substrate can bind to any active site.
The enzyme is permanently changed by binding.
The active site molds slightly to the substrate.
B.why: In induced fit, the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, gripping it more closely.

whyNot.0: It is the active site, not the substrate, that adjusts in the induced-fit model.
whyNot.1: Active sites are specific; only the matching substrate binds.
whyNot.2: The enzyme returns to its original shape and is reused.

B.q: Which reaction would an enzyme named protease catalyze?
options: Breaking proteins into amino acids
Breaking starch into maltose
Breaking fats into fatty acids
Breaking lactose into two sugars
B.why: Enzyme names usually name the substrate: a protease breaks down proteins.

whyNot.1: Breaking starch is the job of amylase.
whyNot.2: Breaking fats is the job of lipase.
whyNot.3: Breaking lactose is the job of lactase.

C.q: Adding much more substrate restores the rate of a reaction slowed by an inhibitor. What does this show about the inhibitor?
options: It binds elsewhere and changes the shape.
It binds the active site and competes.
It has denatured the enzyme permanently.
It has raised the activation energy.
C.why: Only a competitive inhibitor, which competes with the substrate for the active site, can be outcompeted by adding more substrate.

whyNot.0: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere; extra substrate does not overcome it.
whyNot.2: A denatured enzyme would not recover just because more substrate is added.
whyNot.3: Inhibitors block or distort the enzyme; the stem's recovery points to competition for the active site.

C.q: A patient has a fever of 40 °C (104 °F). Why can a very high body temperature disrupt metabolism?
options: Enzymes are used up faster when hot.
Heat raises reactions' activation energy.
Enzymes can denature and lose their shape.
ATP gains an extra phosphate when hot.
C.why: Human enzymes work best near 37 °C. Well above it, they begin to denature: the active site unfolds and reactions slow.

whyNot.0: Enzymes are not consumed at any temperature.
whyNot.1: Temperature does not raise activation energy; the problem is loss of enzyme shape.
whyNot.3: ATP does not gain phosphate groups from heat.

C.q: When ATP is hydrolyzed to power a muscle contraction, which statement about the energy released is accurate?
options: All of it becomes mechanical work.
It is destroyed once the work is done.
It is created as the phosphate breaks off.
Part becomes work and part becomes heat.
C.why: Energy is converted, not created or destroyed, and every conversion loses some energy as heat.

whyNot.0: No conversion is perfectly efficient; some energy is lost as heat.
whyNot.1: Energy cannot be destroyed; it is converted to work and heat.
whyNot.2: Energy cannot be created; it was stored in ATP's phosphate bond.

reteach.title: A tunnel through the hill
reteach.question: Imagine a delivery truck that must cross a steep hill to reach town. How is an enzyme like a tunnel through that hill?

blocks.h: Same start, same finish, lower climb
blocks.body: The trip from one side of the hill to the other is the reaction; the hill is the activation energy. Without a tunnel, few trucks make the climb, so deliveries are slow. A tunnel lets far more trucks through in the same time, but it does not move the town or change how far downhill it sits: the products and the energy released stay the same. The tunnel is not used up by each truck, and if it caves in (denaturation), traffic slows to a crawl again.

blocks.text: A tunnel lowers the climb, not the destination: enzymes lower activation energy but leave the energy released unchanged.

explain.body: Anabolism builds big molecules from small ones and needs energy (protein synthesis, glycogen formation). Catabolism breaks big molecules down and releases energy (respiration, digestion).

options: Breaking polymers and releasing energy
Building polymers and using energy
Breaking polymers and using energy
Building polymers and releasing energy
test.why: Anabolic reactions build larger molecules from smaller ones and require an input of energy.

whyNot.0: Breaking polymers and releasing energy is catabolism.
whyNot.2: Breaking down releases energy rather than using it.
whyNot.3: Building molecules requires energy rather than releasing it.

explain.body: ATP releases energy when its last phosphate is removed (ATP to ADP + Pi). Respiration uses energy from food to reattach the phosphate, recharging ADP into ATP.

test.q: Which molecule is rebuilt from ADP and phosphate using energy from cellular respiration?
options: Glucose
NADPH
AMP
ATP
test.why: Respiration supplies the energy to reattach a phosphate to ADP, regenerating ATP.

whyNot.0: Glucose is the fuel broken down, not the molecule rebuilt from ADP.
whyNot.1: NADPH is an electron carrier made in the light reactions of photosynthesis.
whyNot.2: AMP has one phosphate; adding phosphate to ADP gives ATP.

explain.body: A substrate binds the enzyme's specific active site, the reaction happens with a lower activation energy, the products leave and the unchanged enzyme is reused. Most enzymes are proteins with names ending in -ase.

test.q: Which statement about enzymes is accurate?
options: They raise the activation energy.
They shift a reaction's equilibrium.
They are reused after each reaction.
They are mostly lipid molecules.
test.why: Enzymes leave each reaction unchanged, so one enzyme molecule catalyzes many reactions.

whyNot.1: Enzymes speed the approach to equilibrium but do not move it.

explain.body: Too much heat or the wrong pH denatures it. A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site; a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape. In feedback inhibition, a pathway's end product slows an early enzyme.

test.q: A noncompetitive inhibitor slows an enzyme by:
options: Binding another site and changing its shape
Copying the substrate to fill the active site
Breaking the enzyme's peptide bonds apart
Raising the temperature of the reaction
test.why: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds away from the active site and distorts the enzyme, so extra substrate cannot help.

whyNot.1: Mimicking the substrate and filling the active site is competitive inhibition.
whyNot.2: Inhibitors do not break peptide bonds; they bind to the enzyme.
whyNot.3: Inhibitors are molecules that bind the enzyme; they do not heat the reaction.
